Plain-Language Contract Summary

Section 7 — Indemnification and Limitation of Liability

A non-lawyer's guide to what this section actually means for both parties.

Original request: Summarize the following contract section for a non-technical reader, and define the key legal terms in plain language.

What This Section Does, in Plain Words

Section 7 answers two practical questions: if something goes wrong and someone gets sued or suffers a loss, who pays for it? And is there a ceiling on how much either side can be forced to pay? It has three parts.

7.1 — Who Covers Whose Legal Trouble

Both parties promise to protect each other in the same way (that's what "mutual" means here — it's not a one-sided deal). If Party A causes a problem, Party A has to step in, handle the legal defense, and cover the resulting costs for Party B — and vice versa. This protection kicks in when the problem comes from one of three sources:

  • The party broke a promise it made in the contract.
  • The party did something seriously careless or intentionally wrong.
  • The party's deliverable (software, product, work product, etc.) is accused of stealing or infringing someone else's intellectual property — but only if the deliverable was used the way the contract intended. If the other side modified it, mixed it with outside materials, or used it beyond what was agreed, that protection doesn't apply.

7.2 — The Ground Rules for Handling a Claim

If you're the one being protected and a claim comes in, you must tell the other party promptly (though a late notice only hurts you if it actually caused them harm). You then hand over control of the legal defense to them — they run the case, not you. The one guardrail: they can't settle in a way that admits you did something wrong or forces you to do something (as opposed to just paying money) without your sign-off. You're expected to cooperate along the way, and they cover what that cooperation costs.

7.3 — The Payout Ceiling

This is the section written in all capital letters, which is standard practice for making sure a limitation of liability clause is legally enforceable and hard to miss. It does two things:

  1. Blocks certain damage types entirely. Neither side can collect "indirect" losses — things like lost profits, lost business reputation, or lost data — even if those losses were foreseeable and even if the other side knew they might happen.
  2. Caps total liability. Beyond that, each party's total responsibility for anything related to the contract is capped at whichever is larger: the fees paid in the last 12 months, or $100,000.
The big exception: none of these limits apply to the indemnification promises from 7.1, breaches of confidentiality, gross negligence or willful misconduct, or IP infringement. Those four categories carry uncapped exposure — they carve straight through the liability shield.

Key Legal Terms Defined

Indemnify / Indemnification
To compensate someone for a loss, and to take responsibility for defending them if they get sued over it. Think of it as an insurance-like promise between the two contracting parties themselves.
Hold Harmless
A promise not to let the other party suffer financial harm — usually paired with "indemnify" as a single combined obligation.
Third-Party Claim
A lawsuit or legal demand brought by someone outside the contract — not a dispute between the two companies that signed the agreement, but a customer, competitor, or other outsider suing one of them.
Gross Negligence
Carelessness far beyond an honest mistake — a serious, reckless disregard for consequences that a reasonable person would clearly recognize as dangerous or wrong.
Willful Misconduct
Doing something harmful on purpose, or with knowledge that harm was highly likely — as opposed to an accident or an oversight.
Misappropriate (Intellectual Property)
To use someone else's protected creation — a patent, trademark, trade secret, or copyrighted work — without permission.
Tender Control of Defense
To hand over the steering wheel of a lawsuit to the other party — they choose the lawyers, the strategy, and generally the outcome.
Consequential / Indirect Damages
Losses that are a knock-on effect of a problem, rather than the direct cost of fixing it — e.g., losing a big customer contract because a product broke, rather than just the cost of the broken product itself.
Punitive / Exemplary Damages
Money a court awards not to compensate a loss, but to punish especially bad behavior and discourage others from doing the same thing.
Limitation of Liability
A contract clause that caps how much one party can ever be forced to pay the other, no matter how large the actual damages turn out to be.

Quick Reference: What's Capped vs. Uncapped

Type of LossSubject to the $100k / 12-month Cap?
Indirect, incidental, consequential, punitive damages; lost profits, revenue, goodwill, or dataExcluded entirely — never recoverable, capped or not
Ordinary breach-of-contract damages (general/direct losses)Yes — subject to the cap
Indemnification obligations (Section 7.1)No cap
Confidentiality breaches (Section 9)No cap
Gross negligence or willful misconductNo cap
IP infringement by a partyNo cap
This summary is provided for general understanding only and is not legal advice. Contract language like this can have significant financial consequences, and small wording differences can change outcomes substantially — consult a qualified attorney before relying on this interpretation.
